The story achieves a delicate and effective balance between exteriority and interiority. It grounds the narrative in concrete, observable actions and sensory details (exteriority)—such as Judith lifting the swollen door with her shoulder, pushing the mail aside with her shoe, smelling the caraway-scented soap, and turning on the rusty faucet. Every physical detail naturally triggers memories and unspoken feelings (interiority), such as remembering her father hanging the coat rack too low, her mother picking caraway seeds out of bread, and the realization of the missed appointment on the calendar. By weaving these physical actions seamlessly with her internal reflections, the story conveys a complex, realistic spectrum of emotions—estrangement, nostalgia, grief, and lingering guilt—without ever becoming overly melodramatic or losing the quiet momentum of the scene.
